title: Trump Administration Weighs $100,000 Fee To Stop Foreign Students Working After Graduation
excerpt: The proposed OPT fee would follow the court-blocked $100,000 H-1B levy and directly target Silicon Valley and Wall Street's preferred hiring pipeline from U.S. universities.
body:
• The Trump administration is considering a $100,000 fee on the Optional Practical Training program, which allows roughly 419,000 international graduates to work in the U.S. for one to three years on student visas
  • The proposal follows a federal appeals court in Boston blocking the administration's $100,000 H-1B visa fee last week, and would directly target top Silicon Valley and Wall Street firms that recruit from American universities
  • DHS is also finalizing a new "duration of status" rule, effective September 15, 2026, that replaces open-ended student visa validity with four-year caps and mandatory extension applications
  • Indian students, who form one of the largest international student populations in the U.S., would face compounding barriers to post-graduation employment at a time when applications have already dropped 20%

The Trump administration is weighing a $100,000 fee on international students seeking to work in the United States after graduating from American universities, according to people familiar with the matter, a move that would strike at the heart of what makes U.S. higher education attractive to foreign talent.

The fee would be attached to the Optional Practical Training program, which allows international university graduates to work for one to three years on their student visas. Roughly 419,000 foreigners were working on OPT in 2024, the latest year for which data are available, according to the Wall Street Journal.

"No policies should be considered final until formally announced. At DHS we are always having conversations about how to use all tools in our arsenal to protect the integrity of our legal immigration system."

— Department of Homeland Security spokeswoman

After H-1B Fee Gets Blocked, Focus Shifts to Students

The proposed OPT fee comes in the wake of a federal appeals court in Boston blocking the administration's $100,000 levy on H-1B visas for foreign professionals last week. That fee, introduced through a presidential proclamation in September 2025, had caused widespread alarm in the technology sector before being narrowed to apply primarily to foreign recruits seeking to enter the country from abroad.

https://x.com/NizNellie3/status/2084259823298728187

The new OPT fee would target a different part of the pipeline. Top companies in technology and finance — including firms like Google, Meta, and major Wall Street banks — generally prefer to recruit international talent from U.S. universities and later convert those employees from student visas to H-1Bs. An OPT fee would directly increase the cost of this hiring pathway.

The proposal remains under discussion at the Department of Homeland Security, and it is unclear whether the White House will approve it or who would bear the cost — students, universities, or employers.

Part of a Broader Squeeze on Student Immigration

The fee is one element in what analysts describe as a coordinated strategy to restrict international students' ability to remain in the U.S. after graduation. On July 17, 2026, DHS published a regulation ending the longstanding "duration of status" practice that allowed students to stay in the country for the length of their program plus OPT work authorization.

The new rule, effective September 15, 2026, replaces that flexibility with a four-year cap and requires formal USCIS applications for extensions, transfers between schools, and changes in field of study. A study commissioned by the National Academies of Sciences estimated the regulation could cost the U.S. economy $72 billion to $145 billion annually over ten years.

USCIS Director Joseph Edlow has publicly stated his intention to "significantly limit international students from staying after graduation," and has argued there is "no statutory basis for OPT" — a claim disputed by legal scholars who point to a 1960 congressional exemption of F-1 students from Social Security tax withholding as evidence Congress intended students to work.

Impact on Indian Students

Indian nationals form one of the largest groups of international students in the U.S. and are heavily represented in STEM graduate programs that feed into OPT and eventual H-1B sponsorship. The combination of a potential $100,000 OPT fee, the end of duration of status, and earlier processing pauses on student visa applications has created what immigration advocates describe as an unprecedented level of uncertainty.

International student applications to U.S. universities have already dropped 20%, according to Brookings Institution analysis, with students increasingly choosing Australia, Canada, and the U.K. as alternatives.

Immigration restrictionists argue OPT allows companies to hire foreign graduates without regulations ensuring they are not paid less than American-born graduates. Under the first Trump administration, senior officials including Stephen Miller pushed to abolish STEM OPT but were overruled by more business-oriented members of the team.

What's Next

DHS is separately working on a broader regulation to rewrite OPT rules entirely, expected as soon as this fall. The $100,000 fee idea would likely be attached to a new requirement announced earlier this month that mandates international students apply for visa extensions to use OPT — a departure from the previous system where student visas automatically covered the OPT period.

For the estimated 200,000 Indian students currently enrolled in U.S. universities, the stakes could hardly be higher. The OPT program has long been the bridge between graduation and the U.S. workforce, and any fee of this magnitude would force a fundamental recalculation of whether an American degree remains worth the investment.
